metadata.title: Hudson v. McMillian, 503 U.S. 1 (1992) (No. 90-6531)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Hudson v. McMillian

Opinion filed: 1992-02-25

Docket No.: 90-6531

Citations:
• 117 L. Ed. 2d 156
• 112 S. Ct. 995
• 503 U.S. 1
• 1992 U.S. LEXIS 1372

Case holding summaries:
• "When prison officials maliciously and sadistically use force to cause harm, contemporary standards of decency always are violated. This is true whether or not significant injury is evident."
• describing factors considered in evaluating an excessive force claim
• heightening standard to a "malicious and sadistic" state of mind in certain excessive force cases
• reinstating conviction against prison guard who “expressly condoned the use of force”
• discomfort of prison life part of penalty prisoners pay for their offenses against society
• "society does not expect that prisoners will have unqualified access to health care"
• "Because society does not expect that prisoners will have unqualified access to health care, deliberate indifference to medical needs amount to an Eighth Amendment violation only if those needs are `serious'"
• objective component of excessive force allegation requires only that plaintiff establish he suffered more than de minimis pain or injury; and plaintiff's bruises, swelling, loosened teeth, and a cracked dental plate were more than de minimis injuries for Eighth Amendment purposes
• "The core inquiry for an inmate's Eighth Amendment excessive force claim is `whether force was applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm.'"
• finding that blows which caused bruises, swelling, loosened teeth, and a cracked dental plate were not de minimis for Eighth Amendment purposes
• holding that “the core judicial inquiry” in resolving an Eighth Amendment excessive force claim is “whether force was 2 applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm”
• only deliberate indifference to serious medical needs amounts to an Eighth Amendment violation
• prison officials given wide-ranging deference
• holding that the use of excessive physical force against prisoner may constitute cruel and unusual punishment even though the inmate does not suffer serious injury
• must allege intentional, malicious and sadistic use of force
• excessive force claim tenable in eighth amendment context even without significant injury
• “The Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of cruel and unusual punishments necessarily excludes from constitutional recognition de minimis uses of physical force, provided that the use of force is not of a sort repugnant to the conscience of mankind.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• “[B]lows directed at [Plaintiff], which caused bruises, swelling, loosened teeth, and a cracked dental plate, are not de minimis for Eighth Amendment purposes.”
• explaining the elements of an excessive force claim in the prison context
• "The extent to which a prisoner is injured by the force-indeed, whether he is injured at all-is in the Court's view irrelevant."
• absence of serious injury is relevant to Eighth Amendment inquiry, “but does not end it”
• explaining that “the core judicial inquiry is . . . whether force was applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm”
• requiring both that the alleged wrongdoing was objectively serious enough to establish a constitutional violation and that the prison officials acted with a sufficiently culpable state of mind.
• "In determining whether the use of force was wanton and unnecessary, ... it may also be proper to evaluate the need for application of force ... [and] the threat 'reasonably perceived by the responsible officials.' "
• not every push or shove violates prisoner’s constitutional rights
• prisoner beaten without penological justification
• "The absence of serious injury is ... relevant to the Eighth Amendment inquiry, but does not end it."
• “When prison officials maliciously and sadistically use force to cause harm, contemporary standards of decency always are violated. . . . whether or not significant injury is evident.” (internal citation omitted)
• no excessive force if amount of force commensurate with need therefor
• holding that the Eighth Amendment "necessarily excludes from constitutional recognition de minimis uses of physical force, provided that the use of force is not of a sort repugnant to the conscience of mankind"
• observing that analysis of the objective component in a conditions-of-confinement claim is similar to the objective component of a medical needs case because both require a serious deprivation of needs
• concluding that injuries involving bruises, swelling, loosened teeth, and a cracked dental plate could form the basis of a constitutional violation
• “[E]xtreme deprivations are required to make out a conditions-of-confinement claim.”
• stating that only those deprivations denying the minimal civilized measure of life's necessities are sufficiently grave to form the basis of an Eighth Amendment violation
• holding that “[t]he Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of cruel and unusual punishments necessarily excludes from constitutional recognition de minimis uses of physical force”
• "The absence of serious injury is therefore relevant to the Eighth Amendment inquiry...."
• de minimis use of force does not violate Eighth Amendment unless it is of a sort repugnant to the conscience
• noting “de minimis” uses of physical force are necessarily excluded from Eighth Amendment’s prohibition against “cruel and unusual” punishment
• although not dispositive, "absence of serious injury" is relevant even in excessive force cases
• reversing decision by Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals which required proof of "significant injury" in Eighth Amendment excessive-force cases
• "The Eighth Amendment's prohibition of 'cruel and unusual' punishment necessarily excludes from constitutional recognition de minimus uses of physical force, provided that the use of force is not of a sort repugnant to the conscience of mankind."
• “[T]he core judicial inquiry [in an excessive- force claim] is . . . whether force was applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm.”
• "What is necessary to establish an 'unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain' ... varies according to the nature of the alleged [Eighth Amendment] violation."
• “The absence of serious injury is . . . relevant to the Eighth Amendment inquiry, but does not end it.”
• "society does not expect that prisoners will have unqualified access to health care"
• rejecting suggestion that no Eighth Amendment violation occurs, regardless of the amount of pain inflicted or the evil motives of the responsible prison official, unless the pain is accompanied by significant medical injury
• extent or absence of injury is factor to be considered in determining whether use of force is wanton and unnecessary
• holding Eighth Amendment is violated, even in the absence of serious injury, when guard uses force against prisoner maliciously and sadistically to cause harm, rather than in good-faith effort to maintain discipline
• "When prison officials maliciously and sadistically use force to cause harm, contempo- rary standards of decency always are violated. This is true whether or not significant injury is evident." (citations omitted)
• "Because society does not expect that prisoners will have unqualified access to health care, deliberate indifference to medical needs amounts to an Eighth Amendment violation only if those needs are serious."
